newsitem.title: USA: Gingrich and Nobel laureate disagree on budget.
newsitem.headline: Gingrich and Nobel laureate disagree on budget.

text.p: No one could disagree more about what to do with the federal deficit than House Speaker Newt Gingrich and William Vickrey, the Canadian-born scholar who this week won the Nobel Prize for Economic Science.

Vickrey, a professor emeritus at Columbia University, told Reuters Wednesday that balancing the federal budget would cripple the U.S. economy by sending unemployment soaring to 15 percent and precipitating a Wall Street crash.

Instead, he said, federal policy-makers should gradually raise the deficit to about $500 billion from the $126 billion estimated for the current fiscal year, in order to boost purchasing power and get unemployment to below 1 percent.

The current unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, Vickrey said, arrests Gross Domestic Product at about 12 percent below its potential and isolates the poorest members of society in an economic wasteland of joblessness and crime.

"Now we know that he is an obsolete socialist, representing all the values that collapsed with the Berlin Wall," Gingrich told reporters after a charity breakfast in Atlanta, when asked to comment on Vickrey's viewpoint.
The Georgia Republican pointed to the economic theories of past Nobel laureates Milton Friedman and Gary Becker, who he said believe in balanced budgets and smaller government.

"We can match Nobel prize winners, if you want to. I think people have to decide in their own mind. Is it better to have higher taxes with the money spent in Washington?" said Gingrich, a former community college history professor.

In the presidential campaign, Gingrich's advocacy of a balanced budget has been echoed both by President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole. Deficit reduction, under the Republican plan, would go hand-in-hand with a controversial 15 percent income-tax cut.

Vickrey, who politely refuted Gingrich's "socialist" label by describing himself instead as a follower of famed British economist John Maynard Keynes, said he doubts policy-makers ultimately would eliminate the deficit under any current proposal, Republican or Democrat. But if they did, he said, the consequences could be dire.
"This is my most important piece of work at the moment," the 82-year-old academic said in a telephone interview.
"What I want to do is persuade people this is a danger. And if I can persuade the Washington crowd before the stock market crowd, all will be well."

According to Vickrey's analysis, public debt from the federal, state and local governments serves to equalise a chronic economic imbalance between the demand for assets and the supply of assets. Policy-makers would vastly slow the growth of public debt by eliminating the federal deficit.
The result? "We'll have 15 percent unemployment, or worse," he predicted.

"The deficit is really the net contribution of the government to purchasing power ... Reducing the deficit eventually reduces sales, production and employment ... And so, the programme for reducing the deficit is a programme for increasing unemployment."
He said high unemployment with falling sales and production would be particularly bad at a time when the U.S. stock market has been riding high on "unjustified confidence" in the economy.

Vickrey won half of the $1.12 million Nobel pize for his contribution to the economic theory of incentives, an area of microeconomics that examines decisions different economic players make based on varying amounts of information.
He shared the prize with British professor James Mirrlees of Cambridge University.
